program: Healthy housing remediation, financing and implementation

acceptance.evidence: docs/usa-access-prevention-acceptance.md; independent source/model review and root corrections; initial research, not a qualified pick; docs/geography-central-estimates-acceptance.md

what: GHHI repairs housing hazards and helps public agencies, insurers and local organizations finance and deliver healthier homes.
Its services span lead remediation, asthma trigger reduction, injury prevention, energy upgrades, resident education and policy implementation.
The recipient also manages environmental-health grants, so its ordinary support cannot be treated as an asthma-only intervention.
strengths: Physical home repairs offer a concrete route from an identified hazard to lower exposure or injury risk.
Randomized evidence supports some asthma symptom and recurrent-fall benefits from related home interventions.
Recipient tax returns and a recent consolidated audit reveal spending, partners and the expanding grantmaking portfolio.
reservations: The incremental repairs, public-funding leverage and program mix caused by additional unrestricted support are not identified.
The prominent asthma hospitalization claim is uncontrolled, and lead remediation cannot simply be converted into IQ or lifetime QALYs.
The latest audit consolidates other entities, including a 501(c)(4); it is not the charitable recipient's standalone expense.

sections.what: GHHI's [Maryland services](https://www.greenandhealthyhomes.org/services/maryland-direct-services/) include assessments, hazard remediation, asthma education, energy upgrades, aging-in-place modifications and tenant advocacy. The [2024 recipient return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543189349314709/IRS990) describes direct service and technical-assistance partnerships across US states, alongside policy, data and financing work. Health depends on actual repairs and sustained exposure reduction, not the number of assessments, grant applications or policy announcements.
sections.monitoring: In [2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543189349314709/IRS990), Maryland recorded 875 asthma education/case-management home visits and 234 homes receiving healthy-housing/energy interventions; these are not 875 distinct treated children or 234 asthma-specific completions. Lancaster work included 220 lead-remediated homes and 77 healthy-homes interventions, financed with partners. The return also reports 303 cumulative Molina asthma members and a completed 461-member North Carolina fall-prevention pilot; the latter's payer ROI analysis was still prospective. Recipient-level tracking should identify unique residents, baseline hazards, completed repairs, health outcomes, alternatives, partner expenditure and what additional support changed.
sections.qualitative:
The [Baltimore study](https://www.greenandhealthyhomes.org/wp-content/uploads/GHHI-Improving-Health-Economic-and-Social-Outcomes-through-Integrated-Housing-Intervention-Environmental-Justice.pdf) followed 139 of 201 children with paired caregiver surveys and reported approximately 66% fewer hospitalizations and 28% fewer emergency visits. It had no concurrent control; selection, regression to the mean, seasonality and reporting could explain part of the change. In contrast, [Morgan's randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15356304/) of 937 urban children with atopic asthma found 0.81 fewer symptom days per fortnight in year one and 0.59 in year two. That is a clinical bridge, but generic utility per symptom day and transport to current GHHI clients remain judgments. [Lead-hazard randomization](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6233767/) reduced environmental lead but did not establish broad substantive neurobehavioral improvement. [Home-fall hazard removal](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8408671/) reduced the secondary fall rate, not the primary hazard of first falling or measured quality of life. Neither study licenses assigning every repair a large lifetime health gain. The lead trial enrolled a relatively low-exposure population; its null average neurobehavioral result does not establish zero benefit from targeting severe hazards. GHHI would need its own exposure distribution and sustained reduction before extrapolating larger effects.

Energy and other household-resource pathways were assessed as potentially material and unknown. Historical client utility savings do not identify current marginal household incidence; no zero-income or 90%-health conclusion follows.
sections.cost:
Targeted household resources are assessed unknown. The original asthma-only conditional reference remains about $172 million per ten USA QALYs, with 0.000579837833737864 USA QALYs per $10,000 normalization. This is not a complete combined valuation, zero-income finding, or empirical 90%-health share. All original scenarios and clinical assumptions are preserved.

GHHI's [About Us page](https://www.greenandhealthyhomes.org/about-us/) reports historical Baltimore client energy-cost savings averaging $306 during the first 12 months after intervention. This is meaningful household-resource evidence, but the page does not identify a current unrestricted-gift cohort, baseline bills, comparison group, intervention mix, or joint net costs. The figure cannot be assigned to every modeled asthma child-course. The same page's integrated-delivery efficiencies concern contractor/process costs, not automatically client cash. Cumulative training and reported wage levels likewise do not establish causal retained net earnings from a new gift.

The [Maryland services page](https://www.greenandhealthyhomes.org/services/maryland-direct-services/) shows energy improvements alongside asthma, lead, aging, advocacy and legal services. A future signed-resource ledger needs current gift-responsive unique resource-sharing households and actual utility or private care payments displaced relative to publicly funded or equivalent alternatives. Tenant, owner, landlord, insurer and public-payer incidence must be distinguished. Rent/rate increases, maintenance, energy-use rebound, unreimbursed disruption, travel, administration and time, taxes and benefit withdrawals may offset savings. Full incurred negatives cannot be discounted by asthma response or positive welfare overlap; overlap discounts apply only to gains. Partner, public and capital real-resource costs require separate scope without double counting. Finite delivery, delay, duration and actual net-resource baseline remain unresolved; broader workforce, housing and legal resources are unquantified, not zero.

Our best estimate: About $172 million per 10 USA QALYs through reduced asthma symptoms. At the modeled cost, portfolio allocation and funding response, $10,000 produces about 0.125 additional interventions. Each contributes roughly 0.0047 net QALY before geography, using trial symptom-day reductions, a cautious utility conversion and two years of benefit. We adopt the cautious asthma model: $8,000 per completed intervention, 20% portfolio allocation and 50% funding response. The cost allows a broader contemporary housing bundle than the older trial; allocation is a judgment informed by a mixed portfolio, not a reported asthma spending share. Lead, falls and policy effects remain unpriced, not worthless. Favorable, zero and adverse cases remain in the transparent model; positive scenarios are not confidence bounds or verified funding offers.

The [July 2026 home-electrification case study](https://www.greenandhealthyhomes.org/wp-content/uploads/GHHI_Home-Electrification_Affordability_FINAL.pdf) further illustrates signed uncertainty: four retired homeowners had both bill reductions and increases, with different results after weather and rate normalization. These grant-funded whole-house projects are not the modeled $8,000 child-asthma bundle, and no upfront charge does not guarantee lower ongoing bills. They do not identify the household mix caused by the next unrestricted gift.
sections.funding: The [August 2026-issued audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2025-12-GSAFAC-0000426133) reports $7.89 m unrestricted consolidated net assets, $1.65 m operating cash inflow and $12.32 m financial assets available within a year. It reports $17.10 m federal expenditure, including $8.96 m passed to subrecipients. The [grantmaking page](https://www.greenandhealthyhomes.org/thrivingcommunities/) describes resumed EPA work and a closed application round; it does not establish an unrestricted funding gap. Private support may cover gaps in reimbursable work, but it may also substitute for government, hospital or insurance funding. Contractor capacity, referrals, landlord permission and participant retention matter. [Blue Cross NC's pilot](https://mediacenter.bcbsnc.com/news/blue-cross-nc-and-green-healthy-homes-initiative-team-up-to-reduce-home-injuries-for-leading-cause-of-er-visits-this-fall-season) illustrates why services already financed by an insurer must not all be attributed to philanthropy. No current itemized next-dollar expansion plan was found.

model.costScope: Full charitable recipient support; 2022–24 standalone expense series. Latest consolidated 2025 accounts disclosed separately. Conditional c includes allocated delivery/administration costs, f includes the ordinary-support portfolio share; partner repair costs must be added or explicitly attributed, not treated as free.
model.geographicAttribution: USA-50-states-DC-v 1 residents. Operations are predominantly domestic; g=.99 is a judgment for this narrow direct-service probe, not an observed health-weighted share. Global climate spillovers excluded.
model.formula: Q_USA=(G*b*f/c)*[s*e*(d1+d2/1.03)*u/365-h]*g + G*theta_other; G=10000 computational normalization only. d1=.81*365/14; d2=.59*365/14. theta_other is net USA QALYs per unrestricted dollar from non-overlapping remaining pathways. Cost per 10=10G/Q_USA when positive.
model.counterfactual: b measures additional service spending rather than reserves or replacement funding; s is the fraction of asthma benefit absent without GHHI after landlord, public, insurer and other-provider alternatives. Both are currently judgmental rather than observed. h is incremental disruption or harm relative to the actual alternative. A different, less-disruptive option can deliver equivalent benefit while the extra repair adds harm; identical replacement repairs cancel shared burdens.
model.attribution: f isolates completed asthma remediation from lead, energy, grants, education and policy. e discounts trial transport, adherence and delivery differences. Do not credit public grant face value, partner-financed activity or coalition outcomes in full.
model.uncertainty: We adopt the cautious asthma model: $8,000 per completed intervention, 20% portfolio allocation and 50% funding response. The cost allows a broader contemporary housing bundle than the older trial; allocation is a judgment informed by a mixed portfolio, not a reported asthma spending share. Lead, falls and policy effects remain unpriced, not worthless. Zero and adverse outcomes remain possible; the quantified pathway is not a complete portfolio valuation.
model.nativeOutcomes: Completed and sustained hazard remediations; child symptom-free days; serious falls/injuries; measured exposure changes. Visits, homes, members, grants and dollars saved are not QALYs.

sensitivity: Conditional net asthma gain is 0.0046856 QALY per completed intervention. At b=.5, f=.2, c=$8,000 and g=.99, reaching $1 m per 10 requires 0.8081 QALY per intervention; $100 k requires 8.0808. These are ~172 and ~1,725 times the symptom-only probe.
Holding narrow probe fixed, theta_other must add 0.0000099420 USA QALY/USD to reach $1 m per 10, or 0.0000999420 for $100 k per 10. This is an explicit missing portfolio yield, not a claim it exists.
At the $17.63 m annual recipient cost scale, the $1 m threshold needs about 176.31 net USA QALYs per year and the $100 k threshold about 1,763.07, before any marginal scaling assumption.

Public-funding leverage could improve the donor ratio but requires evidence of additional appropriations or completed repairs, donor causal share and added public resource costs; crowd-out can instead reduce b toward zero.
Do not add avoided hospital bills to QALYs, convert IQ into health without a defensible mapping, or count fall-rate reduction as equivalent mortality reduction.
missingInputs: Current recipient-only financial reconciliation excluding subsidiary and 501(c)(4) spending.
Next-dollar allocation to each program; committed grant coverage; unrestricted gap and contractor/referral bottlenecks.
Completed unique asthma households with all payer costs, severity, sustained repairs and credible comparison care.
Lead exposure reductions by age and baseline level, causal health rather than earnings/IQ bridge, duration and double counting.
Serious injury outcome data and attributable implementation in the 461-member payer pilot; results beyond a before-after ROI forecast.
Environmental subaward and policy portfolio implementation probabilities, causal health exposure changes, geographic health shares and marginal GHHI attribution.

Current marginal gift allocation, unique resource-sharing households and energy intervention mix; actual counterfactual bills and payer/tenant/owner incidence; incremental rent/rate/maintenance/access costs, taxes and benefits; finite delay/duration; net-resource baseline and public/partner implementation scope.

incomeAssessment.rationale: The original organization page reports historical client energy-cost savings, establishing material household-resource potential. Current unrestricted-gift household incidence, intervention mix, counterfactual payments and joint net costs remain unidentified. Unknown is not zero, no material effect, or a 90%-health finding.
directions: Actual household utility or private care payments displaced may increase resources; contractor, insurer, public-payer and landlord savings are not automatically household cash.

Rent or rate increases, maintenance, energy-use rebound and unreimbursed disruption, travel, administration or time can offset savings. Full negative costs remain independent of asthma clinical response.
Taxes, benefit withdrawals, publicly funded alternatives and payer/partner capital or delivery costs require distinct incidence and joint netting; positive overlap applies only to gains.
Workforce, legal advocacy and other portfolio resources remain unquantified; cumulative training and gross wages are not causal next-gift earnings.
